items.elicits: choosing and executing a comparison strategy (common denominator, benchmark, or picture) for 3/4 vs 5/8, and writing the symbol with a reason tied to that method.
choosing and executing a comparison strategy for 2/3 vs 7/12, and writing the symbol with a reason tied to that method.
choosing and executing a comparison strategy for 5/6 vs 8/9 (a pair well suited to near-one/benchmark reasoning), and writing the symbol with a reason tied to that method.

claims.supports: A teacher may conclude the student can choose a valid method (common denominator, benchmark, or visual model), carry it out correctly, and produce a comparison symbol backed by reasoning that matches it, on unlike-denominator pairs they had not seen before.
does_not_support: Does not confirm fluent use of the benchmark-of-one-half strategy specifically as the efficient choice, since all three pairs (3/4 & 5/8; 2/3 & 7/12; 5/6 & 8/9) place both fractions on the same side of 1/2, so common-denominator or near-one reasoning is the more natural route on every item.
Does not confirm comparison of fractions with larger or less-friendly denominators, or ordering more than two fractions at once.

Is easily mistaken for evidence of G5C2's construct-equivalent-fractions procedure: when a student defaults to the common-denominator method on all three items, the same written work partly evidences both claims, and this instrument alone cannot separate 'understands why the symbol follows' from 'can execute the algorithm.'

delegation.reason: The comparison and its supporting reasoning are produced on paper, in the room, individually, with AI excluded, so there is no channel through which the written strategy and symbol could be supplied by someone or something else.

components.component: Chooses a valid strategy (equivalent fractions, benchmark, or visual model)
components.evidence: Part A directs: 'Then show how you know (a common denominator, a picture, or a benchmark like 1/2)', explicitly inviting a strategy choice on all three pairs.
Each item requires 'show how you know', so the executed steps (e.g., common-denominator conversion) are on the page and scorable.
Items 1-3 each require a written '<', '>', or '=' response.

components.component: Shows reasoning that supports (is connected to) the symbol
components.evidence: The instruction 'show how you know' is paired with the symbol on the same item, so alignment between reasoning and symbol is directly scorable.

gate1_components.why: Every component named in G5C1's wording is exercised by items 1-3: each pair forces a strategy choice, visible execution, a symbol, and a reason tied to that symbol. Nothing is absent, so nothing qualifies to be carried forward.

gate2_materiality.why: Not reached: Gate 1 found no absent component to evaluate for materiality.

claims.why_no_intervention: Gate 1 fails: items 1-3 already exercise strategy choice, execution, the resulting symbol, and reasoning tied to that symbol under supervised, novel-number conditions; there is no absent component to carry forward.

items.elicits: finding a common denominator for 1/2 and 1/3, adding the like-sized parts, and reporting the sum.
finding a common denominator for 5/6 and 1/4, subtracting the like-sized parts, and reporting the difference.
converting two mixed numbers to a common denominator, adding whole and fractional parts, and regrouping an improper fraction (13/12) into a mixed number.
applying the common-denominator addition procedure inside a word-problem context and expressing an improper result as a mixed number.
applying the common-denominator subtraction procedure inside a word-problem context.

claims.narrower_inference: Constructs equivalent fractions with a common denominator, and combines or compares the like-sized parts, regrouping an improper result into a mixed number when the arithmetic produces one; recognizing and reducing an already-reducible result to lowest terms is not yet evidenced.
claims.supports: A teacher may conclude the student can find a common denominator for two unlike fractions (including mixed numbers), correctly combine the like-sized parts by addition or subtraction, and regroup an improper fraction into a mixed number when the sum calls for it.
does_not_support: Does not confirm the student recognizes and reduces a non-simplest fraction to lowest terms: none of the six computed results across items 4-9 (5/6, 7/12, 4 1/12, 1 7/12, 5/12, 3/4) needs reduction, so a student could ignore 'simplest form' entirely and still look fully correct.

Is easily mistaken for evidence of G5C1's comparison-reasoning claim when the same common-denominator mechanics appear in both; a correct sum here does not by itself show the student can use that mechanism to justify a comparison symbol.

Does not cover mixed-number subtraction that requires regrouping from the whole number (borrowing), since the only mixed-number item (6) is addition and the subtraction items (5, 8) do not involve mixed numbers.
Does not confirm computational fluency or speed, only correctness with work shown.

delegation.reason: Under proctored, individual, paper/pencil conditions with AI excluded, the 'show every step' requirement makes each step of the computation observable, so the work could not be supplied without the student doing it.

claims.gap_statement: We cannot tell from this assessment whether the student recognizes when a computed fraction is not already in lowest terms and reduces it, because none of items 4-8 (or item 9's corrected sum) produces a result that needs reducing.

components.component: Constructs equivalent fractions with a common denominator
components.evidence: Every item requires converting unlike denominators to a common one before combining (e.g., 1/2+1/3 to sixths, 2 1/3+1 3/4 to twelfths).

components.component: Combines or compares the like-sized parts (correct addition/subtraction)
components.evidence: Each item ends in a required addition or subtraction of the converted like-sized fractions.

components.component: Regroups an improper fraction result into a mixed number
components.evidence: Item 6 (2 1/3+1 3/4=3 13/12) and item 7 (3/4+5/6=19/12) both produce improper fractions that must be regrouped, and item 7 explicitly asks for the answer 'as a mixed number.'

components.component: Reduces a computed result to lowest terms when it is not already in simplest form
components.evidence: Items 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 resolve to 5/6, 7/12, 4 1/12, 1 7/12, and 5/12 respectively -- all already in lowest terms after the common-denominator step -- and item 9's corrected sum (1/2+1/4=3/4) is also already simplest; no item in the assessment forces a reduction step, even though the header instructs 'Answers in simplest form' and the claim names simplification as a required move 'where the item requires it.'

gate1_components.carried_forward: Reduces a computed sum/difference to lowest terms when the result is not already in simplest form
gate1_components.why: This is the only component of G5C2 that is absent: every addition/subtraction instance in the assessment (items 4-9) happens to land on a fraction already in lowest terms, so the 'simplifies' half of 'simplifies or regroups... where the item requires it' is never actually triggered. It belongs to the claim by its own wording, the teacher has not indicated it is assessed elsewhere, and its absence narrows support because the assessment cannot currently distinguish a student who checks-and-reduces from one who does not know that step exists.

gate2_materiality.why: A teacher reading 'answers in simplest form' as an instruction, and seeing every response come out correct in that form, could reasonably conclude students can reduce fractions -- but that conclusion is not carried by this evidence, since no result ever required reducing. The teacher would not otherwise know this, because it takes tracing every computed result across the paper to notice none needs reduction.

gate3_value.why: One short addition item with numbers chosen so the sum lands on a reducible fraction (e.g., 1/6+1/3=3/6, to be written as 1/2) closes the gap directly; it costs under two minutes of class time and a few seconds to score against the rest of a 25-minute assessment that already budgets time for five similar computations (both figures are modeled estimates).

minimum_additional_observation.variant_rule: Keep it a single-step addition of two proper fractions (no mixed numbers, no regrouping) so it isolates reduction from the already-tested regroup skill. Pick any denominator pair with an LCD of 12 or less, matching Part B's difficulty band, such that the computed sum -- before simplifying -- shares a common factor greater than 1 between numerator and denominator (e.g., resulting in 3/6, 4/8, 6/9, or 2/4). Avoid the exact denominator pairs already used in items 4-8 (2&3, 6&4, 3&4, 4&6) so the form stays fresh across periods. The key changes with the chosen pair; scoring checks that the fraction is reduced, not the specific reduced value.
minimum_additional_observation.conditions: Same administration as the rest of the assessment: proctored in class, individual, paper/pencil, AI prohibited -- given as one extra line immediately after Part B rather than as a separate test.
minimum_additional_observation.sufficiency_line: A response counts as evidence if the student reduces the computed sum to lowest terms (1/2), not left as an unreduced equivalent (3/6) or any other unreduced form.

items.elicits: locating the specific error in a given incorrect solution (denominators added directly: 1/2+1/4 read as (1+1)/(2+4)=2/6), explaining in words why that produces a wrong-sized part, and computing the correct sum by a valid common-denominator method.

claims.supports: A teacher may conclude the student can recognize that adding denominators directly changes the size of the fractional parts, explain that specific misconception in their own words, and produce the correct sum for that problem.
does_not_support: Does not confirm the student would catch this same error in their own original work rather than in a mistake already flagged for them -- self-monitoring during independent problem-solving is a different, untested skill.

Does not generalize to other wrong-denominator or wrong-numerator errors (e.g., multiplying denominators incorrectly, or adding numerators only), since only the one named bug (1/2+1/4 -> 2/6) is presented.

Does not by itself guarantee the explanation names the wrong-sized-part cause specifically rather than a generic 'he made a mistake,' unless the rubric requires the size-based reason -- the item invites it but a vague explanation could still earn credit for the 'correct sum' half.
Does not confirm the student can generate a common-denominator solution unprompted, from scratch, without an already-flagged error to react to (that skill is G5C2's territory).

delegation.reason: The explanation and the corrected sum are written on paper in the room, individually, with AI excluded, so the diagnostic reasoning could not be produced without the student doing it.

components.component: Locates/identifies the specific error (denominators added directly)
components.evidence: Item 9 presents the exact bug (1/2+1/4 -> 2/6, which is (1+1)/(2+4)) and asks 'Explain what the student did wrong.'

components.component: Explains why that action produces a wrong-sized part
components.evidence: The 'Explain what the student did wrong' prompt directly invites the size-based reasoning named in the claim.
Item 9 explicitly also asks the student to 'show the correct answer.'

gate1_components.why: Item 9 is a direct, purpose-built match to G5C3: the presented bug is exactly 'adding denominators' named in the claim, and its two-part prompt exercises locating the error, explaining the size-based cause, and giving the correct sum in one response. A component exercised once counts as present, so nothing here is absent.

gate2_materiality.why: Not reached: Gate 1 found no absent component to evaluate for materiality.

claims.why_no_intervention: Gate 1 fails: item 9 already exercises every component of G5C3 -- locating the error, explaining why it produces a wrong-sized part, and giving the correct sum -- in a single supervised, purpose-built item; there is no absent component to carry forward.

conditions_echo: Grade 5 mathematics, end of Unit 4, summative, proctored in class, individual work, paper and pencil only, AI prohibited and enforced, 25 minutes; students have practiced this item type before but these specific numbers and problems are new to them -- so independence and novelty hold for every item on this instrument.
reviewer_notes: Because supervision is proctored_in_class and the teacher's novelty note confirms the specific numbers/problems are new, independence and novelty are satisfied assessment-wide; the analysis below turns on claim-targeting and whole-claim coverage. G5C1 (comparison strategy and reasoning) and G5C3 (diagnose the added-denominators error) are each already fully carried by their matched items and warrant no changes. G5C2 (construct/combine/simplify-or-regroup) is carried in substance for construction, combination, and regrouping, but every addition/subtraction instance in the assessment -- items 4 through 9 -- happens to resolve to a fraction already in lowest terms, so the 'simplify' half of the claim is never actually triggered despite the header instruction 'Answers in simplest form.' One short added item (a single addition whose sum needs reducing) closes that gap without touching anything else in the instrument.
